passage:
"You forgot my birthday, Sahil. Even Mummy's cousin in Canada remembered."
Sahil put his phone down. "I'm sorry, Lavu. I got caught up with the match."
"You always get caught up."
He opened his mouth to defend himself, then stopped. "You're right. I keep saying sorry and then doing it again."
Lavanya crossed her arms. "So?"
"So I've been thinking about what kind of brother I want to be. Not the one who remembers because Mummy reminds him."
"Then what kind?"
"The kind you can count on. When you have exams, I'll do your chores. And I'm putting your birthday in my calendar for the next ten years."
Lavanya almost smiled. "Eleven."

qa.q: Why did Sahil say he forgot the birthday?
qa.a: He got caught up with the match.

qa.q: Why did Sahil stop himself from defending himself?
qa.a: He felt sorry, realising Lavanya was right about his pattern, and wanted to own it instead of making excuses.

qa.q: What makes Sahil's promise more believable than a plain sorry?
qa.a: He named specific actions, like doing her chores during exams and putting the date in his calendar.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's "Eleven" suggest about how she sees him now?
qa.a: She is softening and willing to give him a chance, teasing him as a sign the hurt is easing. 🙂

grounding: It shows a teenager deciding what kind of brother he wants to be after letting his sister down.

passage: Last winter Sangeeta told me her parents were fighting a lot and she was sleeping at her aunt's. Two other people in our group asked, "Lalit, what's going on with her?" and I realised I had a choice. I could be the guy who knows things and passes them on, which, honestly, I used to be. Or I could be something else. I told them, "Ask her if you want to know." Then I just kept showing up. Walking her to the bus. Not asking too much. I think that's when I figured out what kind of friend I want to be: the one people can tell things to without it going anywhere. It changed how I see myself, not just her.

qa.q: Where was Sangeeta sleeping?
qa.a: At her aunt's.

qa.q: What choice did Lalit feel he faced when others asked about Sangeeta?
qa.a: Lalit felt torn between staying the guy who passes things on and becoming a friend who keeps things private.

qa.q: What could Lalit also do if Sangeeta seemed very low for a long time?
qa.a: Gently encourage her to talk to a trusted adult or the school counsellor, while still being there as a friend.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta experience Lalit "just showing up"?
qa.a: As steady, quiet support that doesn't make her explain or relive things. 🤍

grounding: It shows a teenager choosing the kind of friend he wants to be when a friend confides in him.

passage: School counsellor's note, Aparna. Reena, fifteen, came to talk again today. She said she has always been "the easy friend": agreeing to every plan, lending notes, never saying no. Last week she lent her project file and got it back torn, and she said nothing. Today she said, "I want to be a good friend, but I don't want to disappear." We talked about what she values: loyalty, honesty, fun. She wrote a line on a sticky note: "Kind, not a doormat." She plans to tell her friend about the file, calmly. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What happened to the project file Reena lent?
qa.a: It came back torn.

qa.q: What did Reena mean by "I don't want to disappear"?
qa.a: She was worried that always agreeing was making her lose herself, and she wanted her own needs to count in friendships too.

qa.q: Why is telling her friend about the file calmly a good first step?
qa.a: It lets Reena practise speaking up in a small, specific situation without ending the friendship.

qa.q: How might Reena's friend react when Reena mentions the file?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since Reena never complained before, but it could also make the friendship more honest.

grounding: It shows, in a counsellor's note, a teenager deciding what kind of friend she wants to be.

passage: Tuesday night. Something small happened today but I can't stop thinking. At lunch the girls were laughing about Dilnaz's new haircut and I laughed too, and even added a joke. Then Dilnaz walked in and sat next to me like normal, and I felt sick. She has been my friend since Class 3. When Ammi was in hospital last year, Dilnaz came every evening with my notes. And I sold her out for one laugh. I don't want to be like that. I want to be the one who says 'leave it' even if it's awkward. Tomorrow I'll tell her, maybe not everything, but that I was mean and I'm sorry. And next time I'll actually say 'leave it' out loud. – Parveen

qa.q: Since which class has Dilnaz been Parveen's friend?
qa.a: Since Class 3.

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel sick when Dilnaz sat next to her?
qa.a: Parveen felt guilty for having just joked about a friend who had always been loyal.

qa.q: What would you advise Parveen for tomorrow?
qa.a: Apologise simply and honestly, then show the change by speaking up the next time the group mocks someone.

qa.q: If you were Dilnaz, what would you want from Parveen?
qa.a: I would want an honest apology and to know Parveen will stand by me when I'm not in the room. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of friend she wants to be after letting a loyal friend down.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager choosing what kind of older sister she wants to be, modelled on her cousin.

passage: Eshaan, sixteen, came back from the village school in a foul mood and snapped at his little sister Charu when she asked for help with her maths. She went quiet and did it alone. That night, lying on the charpai under the stars, he thought about his own older cousin, who used to shout at him and whom he still avoided at weddings. He didn't want to be that. The next morning he sat beside Charu at breakfast. "Sorry about yesterday. Show me the sums." She blinked, then pushed the notebook over. He decided then: he would be the brother she could come to.

qa.q: Where was Eshaan lying when he thought about his cousin?
qa.a: On the charpai under the stars.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling as he thought about his older cousin?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, not wanting to repeat how his cousin had treated him.

qa.q: What small step did Eshaan take toward the brother he wants to be?
qa.a: He apologised and offered to help Charu with her sums the next morning.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Eshaan apologises?
qa.a: Surprised and relieved, and more willing to come to him again.

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of brother he wants to be after hurting his sister.

passage: In Amsterdam, Sami, fifteen, heard that his friend Yosef's parents were splitting up. Yosef hadn't said a word; he'd just stopped coming to football. Sami thought about the friends who'd drifted away when his own grandfather died, and the one who'd kept showing up with bad jokes and snacks. He knew which one he wanted to be. So on Saturday he cycled to Yosef's flat with a bag of crisps. "You don't have to talk," he said. They played video games for three hours in near silence. Before Sami left, Yosef said, "Come next week?"

qa.q: What did Sami bring to Yosef's flat?
qa.a: A bag of crisps.

qa.q: What was Sami thinking about when he decided to visit?
qa.a: He remembered feeling hurt by friends who drifted away and grateful for the one who stayed, and wanted to be like that one.

qa.q: What did Sami's approach get right?
qa.a: He showed up without pressure, letting Yosef decide whether to talk.

qa.q: How might Yosef feel when Sami says he doesn't have to talk?
qa.a: Relieved and cared for, without being pushed to explain.

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of friend he wants to be when a friend is going through a hard time.

passage: In the college hostel, Nilesh, seventeen, overheard two boys laughing about his roommate Raghav's accent and his old phone. One of them turned to Nilesh. "You share a room with him, right? Tell us something funny." Nilesh felt the pull to join in, to be one of them. He also remembered how Raghav had stayed up to help him with physics. "Nothing funny," he said. "He's a good roommate." The boys shrugged and moved on. Back in the room, Nilesh didn't mention it. But he realised he'd just decided something about the kind of friend he wanted to be.

qa.q: What were the two boys laughing about?
qa.a: Raghav's accent and his old phone.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when the boys asked him for something funny?
qa.a: He felt tempted to fit in, but also loyal to Raghav, and uncomfortable with the mockery.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying "He's a good roommate" ended the gossip without a fight and kept his loyalty.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel if he ever learned what Nilesh said?
qa.a: Deeply grateful and more trusting of him as a friend.

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of friend he wants to be when tempted to mock his roommate.

passage:
Zainab,
I'm writing this because I'm bad at saying things out loud. When you told me about not getting into the choir, I made a joke. I thought it would help. It didn't. I saw your face. I've been thinking a lot about what kind of friend I want to be. My cousin is the kind of friend who's fun but disappears when things get hard. I don't want to be that. I want to be someone people can tell stuff to without worrying I'll laugh. So I'm sorry. If you want to talk, I'll just listen this time. And if you ever want someone older to talk to, the counsellor, Mrs Das, is good. I went to her last year.
Vaibhav

qa.q: Who does Vaibhav recommend Zainab could talk to?
qa.a: The counsellor, Mrs Das.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel after making the joke?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt guilty and regretful, having seen Zainab's face.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do if Zainab wants to talk?
qa.a: Listen without joking, as promised, and gently remind Zainab about the counsellor if things feel too much.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Zainab may feel relieved and more able to trust Vaibhav again.

grounding: A teenager writes an apology letter to a friend, deciding what kind of friend to be.

passage: "Okay, so the school radio asked me what I've learned this year. I'm Urmila, Class 11. The honest answer is about my sister, Shreya. She's twelve. I used to boss her around, like, all the time. Then in March she didn't tell me something important, she told our neighbour instead. That hurt. I asked her why, and she said, 'Because you always shout.' I sat on the terrace that night and thought, what kind of didi do I actually want to be? Not the one she hides from. So now I try to ask before I lecture. I still mess up. Last week I shouted about my charger. But she told me about her exam fear yesterday. That felt like winning something."

qa.q: How old is Shreya?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when Shreya told the neighbour instead?
qa.a: Urmila felt hurt and shaken, realising Shreya didn't trust her.

qa.q: What change is Urmila trying to make as a sister?
qa.a: Asking before lecturing, so Shreya feels safe to share things.

qa.q: How might Shreya see the change in Urmila?
qa.a: Shreya seems to be starting to trust her again, telling her about the exam fear.

grounding: A teenage girl describes deciding what kind of older sister she wants to be.

passage: I'm Wasim, Vishal's cousin. We're both fifteen. When our grandfather came home from hospital, Vishal changed. Before, he'd come to Nana's only for festivals, eat, and play on his phone. Now he comes every Sunday. He sits with Nana on the balcony and reads him the newspaper, even the boring parts. Once I asked why, and he said, "I don't want to be the grandson who only shows up for sweets." Then he shrugged like it was nothing. He also started calling his mother from hostel every night. I don't know what exactly changed inside him, but he seems quieter and older, somehow.

qa.q: What does Vishal read to Nana on the balcony?
qa.a: The newspaper, even the boring parts.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling when he shrugged after answering Wasim?
qa.a: He may have felt a little shy or embarrassed about how much it mattered to him.

qa.q: What could Wasim do if he wants to support this change?
qa.a: Wasim could join Vishal on some Sundays with Nana, rather than teasing Vishal about it.

qa.q: How does Wasim see his cousin's change?
qa.a: Wasim notices Vishal seems quieter and older, though Wasim can't know exactly what changed inside.

grounding: A cousin observes a teenager decide to become a more caring grandson and son.

passage:
Before: When Irawati cancelled their movie plan for the third time, Aparna typed a sharp message and deleted it. She sent "whatever 👍" instead and went quiet for a week. That was how her older cousins handled friends: cut them off before they cut you.
During: On Friday, Irawati's little brother mentioned their grandmother was in hospital. Aparna felt her stomach drop. Irawati hadn't said a word.
After: The next Monday Aparna walked over at lunch. "I'm sorry I went cold. I want to be the kind of friend who asks first." Irawati's eyes filled. "I didn't know how to say it."
That evening Aparna wrote in her notebook: ask before assuming. Show up. She decided that was the friend she meant to be.

qa.q: What did Aparna first send Irawati?
qa.a: She sent "whatever 👍" and went quiet for a week.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel on Friday when she heard about the grandmother?
qa.a: She felt guilty and shaken; her stomach dropped because she had gone cold on Irawati without knowing.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Aparna assumed the worst and cut Irawati off; next time she can ask what is going on before reacting.

qa.q: What was it like for Irawati during that week?
qa.a: Irawati was dealing with a grandmother in hospital and felt unable to explain, while her friend had gone silent.

grounding: Shows a teen choosing what kind of friend she wants to be after a misjudged cut-off.

passage:
Sit, Manjula. You asked why I still phone my brother every Sunday even though we fight.
When I was about fifteen, my brother and I shared one room and one cycle. I was mean to him. I hid the cycle key, I told Amma his secrets. I thought that was simply how older sisters behaved.
Then one night he had a high fever and Amma was on night shift. I sat with him, wiping his forehead, and he whispered, "Thank you, didi." Nobody had ever thanked me for being kind to him, because I never had been.
Next morning I gave him the key. I decided then: I would be a sister he could count on, even when he annoyed me.
So I, Sharmila, phone every Sunday. That is the sister I chose.

qa.q: What did Sharmila hide from her brother?
qa.a: She hid the cycle key.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have felt when her brother whispered thank you?
qa.a: She likely felt touched and ashamed at once, because nobody had thanked her for kindness she had never shown before.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Sharmila's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sitting with her brother during his fever; it showed her what kind of sister she could be and led her to give him the key.

qa.q: How might the brother have felt when he got the key back the next morning?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and relieved, seeing his sister begin to treat him differently.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding, as a teen, what kind of sister she wanted to be.

passage:
Himani had forty minutes before the last bus and a promise to keep. Nilesh, her friend since Class 3, had asked her to come to his first stage play at the community hall. Her mother had also asked her to be home for her cousin's engagement dinner.
The rain started as she left school. Autos were full. She ran through puddles and reached the hall soaked, just as the curtain rose. She watched his first scene from the back, clapped hard, then slipped out to catch the bus.
She texted him: "Saw you. You were brilliant. Couldn't stay, family dinner, tell me everything tomorrow."
On the bus she thought about it. She didn't have to choose one person over another. She could be someone who shows up, even for part of it, and tells the truth about why.

qa.q: How much time did Himani have before the last bus?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Himani seem to feel on the bus afterwards?
qa.a: She felt settled and a bit relieved that she had kept both promises in part and been honest with Nilesh.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Going for the first scene and texting Nilesh the truth worked, because she showed up for her friend and still kept her family commitment.

qa.q: If you were Nilesh, what would you want from Himani's text?
qa.a: You would likely feel seen and happy that she came in the rain, and look forward to telling her everything tomorrow.

grounding: Shows a teen deciding what sort of friend and family member she wants to be under time pressure.

passage: On the metro home from coaching class in Delhi, Zubin was quiet. Usually Amandeep filled silences with jokes, and usually Zubin laughed. Today Zubin said, "My parents are separating. Dad's moving out on Sunday." Amandeep opened his mouth to crack something, anything, then shut it. He thought of his cousin Harjot, who always just sat with him when things went wrong at home, and how much that had mattered. "I'll come over Sunday," Amandeep said. "We don't have to talk. I'll bring the chess set." Zubin nodded, eyes on the window. That night Amandeep typed into his phone notes: Be the friend who shows up. Less joking, more staying.

qa.q: When is Zubin's dad moving out?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep shut his mouth instead of cracking a joke?
qa.a: He felt concerned for Zubin and sensed a joke would be wrong, remembering how much quiet support had comforted him.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do on Sunday to live out his note?
qa.a: He could turn up as promised, play chess, and let Zubin decide whether to talk.

qa.q: What might Amandeep's offer mean to Zubin?
qa.a: Zubin probably feels less alone, knowing a friend will be there on a hard day without pressure to talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of friend he wants to be when a friend is going through a hard time.
